A_target.statement:
Let $n \in \Z_{>1}$.
Then $\Z / n \Z$ is a [[Definition:Commutative Ring with Unity|commutative ring with unity]], and it is a [[Definition:Field (Abstract Algebra)|field]] {{iff}} $n$ is [[Definition:Prime Number|prime]].

B_source.statement: $\struct {\Z, +, \times}$ is an [[Definition:Integral Domain|integral domain]]: a commutative ring with unity, cancellation, and no [[Definition:Zero Divisor of Ring|zero divisors]].

substitutions.integer addition and multiplication: the same operations computed on representatives

derived.the ring identities: transferred unchanged, since congruence is compatible with the operations
derived.cancellation and absence of zero divisor: lost for composite n, where nonzero classes can multiply to zero

validity_conditions: The operations are well defined on classes because congruence is compatible with addition and multiplication, so every ring identity transfers.
Cancellation fails for composite n: a proper factorization gives two nonzero classes whose product vanishes, so the ring has zero divisors.
Order does not transfer at all, since congruence classes have no compatible ordering; inequalities between integers have no modular counterpart.
proof_plan: Replace each integer $a$ by its [[Definition:Residue Class|residue class]] $\eqclass a n$.

If $a \equiv a'$ and $b \equiv b' \pmod n$, then $a + b \equiv a' + b'$ and $a b \equiv a' b' \pmod n$.
Hence addition and multiplication are well-defined on classes, by [[Congruence Modulo Integer is Congruence Relation]].
The ring axioms hold in $\Z / n \Z$, as each is an identity already true in $\Z$.

If $n = a b$ with $1 < a, b < n$, then $\eqclass a n \eqclass b n = \eqclass 0 n$, so cancellation fails.
If $n$ is prime, $\eqclass a n \ne 0$ implies $a \perp n$, and [[Bézout's Identity]] gives an inverse.
The ordering of $\Z$ does not transfer at all.
{{qed}}
